title: Why Does setState Work Asynchronously?
text:
This is less an attempt to memorize the “correct answer” to an interview
question than a record of following that question into the way React defines
state updates and rendering—and the choices it made to solve the problems it
found there.

I usually like writing whose overall structure is visible from the beginning.
Each paragraph should stay close to its subject, and the reader should have a
natural sense of where they are. This article takes a slightly different path.
“Why does setState work asynchronously?” is not a summary of the whole
article so much as its entrance. Follow it carefully and it leads into rendering
models, priority, user experience, and concurrency—like a small opening to an
anthill that reveals a surprisingly deep structure once you start digging.

We will begin at that entrance and trace why React chose not to apply state
immediately, and what that choice eventually made possible.

Part 1: Because It Is a More Efficient Structure

There is no single reason setState developed into its current form. The design
is better understood as several decisions, made from different perspectives,
overlapping to produce the structure we use today.

That is also why a new concept can feel like an ocean with no visible shore.
“Why was it designed this way?” often cannot be answered with one reason. But
when you approach the question from several directions, those perspectives
eventually converge into an “aha” moment. We will look at setState in the same
way.

 

Begin with a simple assumption: what if calling setState changed the state
and redrew the screen immediately?

At first, that sounds direct and intuitive. Change the state and the UI changes.
But the model reaches its limits quickly:

- React is rendering component A.
- setState is called halfway through that work.
- The state changes immediately.

What should React do with the UI it has already calculated? It could throw the
work away and restart, or inject the new state into the middle of the existing
calculation. Neither is elegant. Rendering becomes an unpredictable computation
whose conditions keep changing while it runs.

React's basic view of rendering is mathematical:

 UI = f(state, props)

Rendering is not merely drawing pixels. It is the computation that receives the
current state and props as inputs and determines what UI should exist. The
important premise is that the same input should always produce the same
result.

If state changes halfway through the calculation, the function can no longer be
trusted. A function that continues with externally changed inputs is difficult
to predict and just as difficult to optimize.

Safe rendering therefore requires its inputs to remain stable while the
calculation is in progress. React separates this work into a Render Phase, which
calculates UI from state and props, and a Commit Phase, which applies the result
to the DOM and runs effects. Side effects are forbidden during the Render Phase
because this phase is only a calculation.

Seen in that context, “apply the update on the next cycle” has a precise
meaning: the update does not change the current calculation; it becomes an
input to the next render.

The asynchronous behavior of setState is therefore not merely a performance
trick. It is a structural choice that makes rendering a safe computation.

 

Consider this code:

From an imperative point of view, it looks like three updates. React, however,
is ultimately less interested in how many intermediate steps occurred than in
the final question: given the resulting state, what UI should it calculate?

Calculating once with only A changed, again with A and B changed, and then a
third time with A, B, and C changed repeats work whose intermediate results are
not useful. React therefore collects updates and discards unnecessary
intermediate calculations. What we call batching is a prerequisite for this
computational model.

 

What makes a good UI? A UI is not necessarily good just because it changes as
quickly as possible.

A list that jumps during scrolling, a page that flashes or freezes while
typing, or an interface that shows no response after a click can all result when
every small state change immediately triggers rendering. The render calculation
interrupts the user's interaction.

For user experience, “could the user keep acting without interruption?” matters
more than “how quickly did something change?”

- During typing, typing should take priority.
- Immediately after a click, feedback is important.
- During a page transition, some work can arrive slightly later.

React can make these distinctions only if rendering does not have to execute
immediately. When every update has the same importance, there is no way to
choose what matters now.

This stability matters to developers too. When state is applied immediately,
update timing is scattered and render results become harder to reconstruct
mentally. When updates are collected and applied together, debugging and
reasoning become simpler.

So the asynchronous behavior of setState is not only a performance decision.
It gives users an uninterrupted experience and developers a predictable model.

Part 2: Optimization for a Smoother User Experience

Part 1 explained why collecting updates is safer and more predictable than
rendering immediately after every state change. One problem remains: collecting
work does not guarantee a good experience if the calculation itself takes a
long time. Even a batched render can still leave the user staring at a frozen
screen.

 

In a simple React application, blocking rendering—finishing a render in one
uninterrupted pass—is rarely a problem. The component tree is small, state
changes are limited, and Virtual DOM diffing is fast.

The problem becomes visible when an application filters or sorts thousands of
items. The interface begins to stutter, and a technical detail becomes a user
experience problem. Debounce and throttle can hide some symptoms, but they do
not remove the underlying limitation.

 
   
    Your browser does not support the video element.
   
   
    Source:{" "}
     
      Stress Testing Concurrent Features in React 18
     
   
 

In the video, the SearchBar does not respond as the user types. It freezes and
then applies several characters at once. The 3D scene on the same screen drops
frames as well, making the entire UI feel blocked.

The Performance panel shows a large task for each keypress. For every input,
React calculates the next result for both SearchBar and Scene, occupying the
main thread for a long stretch. The longest task takes almost 0.8 seconds.
During that time JavaScript owns the main thread, the browser cannot do other
work, and user input cannot be processed. That is why the page feels slow.

 

Before React 18, React treated rendering as a comparatively simple scheduling
problem. It asked how urgent an update was and encoded both priority and
batching in a numeric Expiration Time.

Representative constants looked like this:

See the React 16.12 source.

The names and values carry several historical meanings because expirationTime
was used differently by the scheduler and reconciler. The important point here
is simply that React assigned every update a numeric value. That value
simultaneously represented:

- the update's priority,
- which updates should be grouped into the same batch, and
- how much work should be included in a render.

Larger values represented more urgent work. Updates with the same expiration
time were treated as belonging to the same event flow. React could therefore
decide which priority to process now and skip less urgent subtrees during that
render.

Looking back from modern React, the limits are clear:

- Every decision is a linear numeric comparison.
- Priority, batching, and inclusion are tightly coupled in one number.
- A completed render is always expected to reach the screen eventually.
- Rendering is synchronous: if priority is A  B  C, React cannot work on B
  before A finishes, or on C before both A and B finish.

When the only problem was deciding what to draw first, these were not really
limitations. The simpler model was sufficient.

 

Suspense formally introduced a new rendering state: UI that is not ready
yet. Previously, IO-bound delays such as network, file, or asynchronous
requests were usually handled outside rendering with branches such as
isLoading. With Suspense, React may discover during rendering that required
data or code is not ready.

React can stop that render instead of forcing it to completion, commit a
fallback, and retry when the dependency becomes available. The rendering model
therefore expanded to include IO-bound delays, suspension, scheduling, and
resumption.

This exposed the limits of Expiration Time. Because the model converted priority
into a deadline, nearby updates with the same priority tended to share similar
expiration values. After Suspense, however, rendering naturally moves through
suspended, retried, and partially committed states. One update may be blocked
on data while another can proceed. A single time value cannot precisely express
whether work is possible, blocked, or ready to retry.

React 18 also needed different strategies for transitions, Suspense boundaries,
and hydration. Updates had to be classified and scheduled at a finer
granularity.

 

The problem can now be summarized like this:

- A render can start without completing.
- A render in progress can become obsolete.
- Some renders should wait, while others should be abandoned.

A purely synchronous rendering model cannot satisfy these conditions. The
problem is no longer only computation speed; it is how time should be shared.
Concurrency provides the solution.

 
   Concurrency vs. Parallelism 
   
    

    Parallelism executes multiple operations at the same time. Concurrency
    divides two or more independent tasks into pieces and switches between them
    so they appear to progress together. It does not require multiple JavaScript
    threads, but it does require context switching.

    - Concurrency is about dealing with multiple independent tasks at once;
      parallelism is about executing related operations at the same instant.
    - Concurrency describes how to structure several tasks; parallelism
      describes how to run several tasks simultaneously.

   
 

Concurrency is a useful answer because rendering is CPU-bound. Running component
functions, calculating hooks, constructing a Fiber tree for diffing, and
determining DOM changes are all computations. They execute synchronously on the
main thread. As lists grow, trees deepen, or updates cascade, the work can
stretch from a few milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, delaying input and
scrolling.

JavaScript is single-threaded and React rendering is JavaScript work, so React
cannot simply await it or send it to a background thread. Instead of making
the calculation itself asynchronous, React made rendering interruptible,
resumable, and disposable.

The React 18 announcement
describes concurrency as a behind-the-scenes mechanism that lets React prepare
multiple versions of the UI at the same time. “Prepare” is the revealing word:
React can calculate more than one possibility and choose the most appropriate
result.

All of this builds on the decision from Part 1. If setState forced a render
immediately, React could not divide, pause, resume, or discard that work.

Part 3: The Lane Model for Finer-Grained Rendering

 

The weakness of Expiration Time was not simply a lack of priority levels. It was
that unrelated decisions—priority, deadline, and batching—were tightly coupled
to one number.

Real UI interactions rarely have only one meaning. A single keystroke in a
search field may create several updates:

- The input value should appear immediately.
- Search results can arrive slightly later.
- A render for an older query may be discarded.

Updates with different priorities and different fates coexist in one flow.
Trying to express them as a single line creates a natural limit. React instead
treats pending work as a set that can contain several Lanes at once, using a
bitmask as its representation.

Conceptually:

Internally, the set can be represented like this:

00000101 means that synchronous work and lower-priority transition work are
both waiting. A bitmask expresses this coexistence directly, and bit operations
make set operations cheap:

These operations run in O(1) time and use little memory. During rendering, React
can quickly determine which kinds of updates remain and which should be handled
first.

 

The Lane definitions include groups such as:

The main categories are:

- SyncLane: discrete physical interactions processed individually, such as
  click, input, mouse down, and submit.
- InputContinuousLane: continuous interactions such as drag, scroll, mouse
  move, and wheel.
- DefaultLane: other updates, including updates originating outside React,
  such as setTimeout and Promise callbacks.
- TransitionLane: transitions marked by the developer through
  startTransition() or useTransition().

Event priority maps to the corresponding Lane:

DOM events are then classified:

 

Step 1 — An update receives a Lane

When setState is called, React first determines the kind of event that caused
the update and selects a Lane:

- User input such as a click or keystroke → SyncLane
- Work inside startTransition → TransitionLane
- A Suspense retry → RetryLane
- Connecting server-rendered HTML → HydrationLane

The Lane is attached to the update like metadata and stored in the Fiber's
update queue:

Rendering has not started yet. At this point the Lane records the intention:
what priority and behavior should this update have?

Step 2 — Scheduling chooses the Lane set to process now

React collects pending updates at the root:

It uses getHighestPriorityLane(pendingLanes) and
getNextLanes(root, wipLanes) to determine what can run:

This isolates the rightmost 1 bit—the highest-priority Lane—and establishes
the reference point for the render. React then calculates which Lane set is
actually available:

The result becomes renderLanes, the Lane set used for the current render.

Step 3 — Rendering checks whether each update belongs

As React traverses the Fiber tree, it checks whether an update's Lane is
included in the current renderLanes:

- Included → apply it in this render.
- Not included → skip it and continue through the tree.

Consider a single keystroke that creates two updates:

- query: the input value must appear immediately → SyncLane
- results: filtering and list rendering can wait → TransitionLane

The root accumulates both:

The scheduler chooses the highest-priority work:

The query update belongs to renderLanes, so React applies it and commits the
new input value quickly. The results update does not belong, so it is skipped
for now and the previous results remain visible.

If the user continues typing re, then rea, each keystroke adds urgent
SyncLane work. Even if a TransitionLane render has started, the urgent work
can interrupt it. The old transition result is now obsolete and can be
discarded. From the user's perspective, input remains responsive and the
results eventually update only for the newest query.

 

Why is setState asynchronous, and why is its result applied on a later cycle?

It is not simply a performance optimization. React treats rendering as
schedulable work rather than an operation that must execute immediately.
Early React finished each render synchronously, but as applications grew, long
renders blocked input and dropped frames. React therefore stopped treating a
setState call as an instruction to render at once and began deciding when and
at what priority the update should be processed.

The Lane model classifies updates by priority and purpose. User input can be
urgent while filtering a large list can be deferred. Updates created by the
same event do not all have to be handled in the same render; React can process
the important work first.

It is more accurate, then, to say that React examines the pending work and
applies each update at the most appropriate time. Because state is not forced
onto the screen immediately, React can interrupt, restart, or discard renders
while preserving input responsiveness in complex interfaces.

title: A History of React Rendering Strategies
text:
Presented for the NAVER Cloud frontend study on May 30, 2025   updated
  March 11, 2026.
 

Why I Chose This Topic

- I think understanding how React has evolved helps us design better code and structure with a tool we use every day.
- I want to see React 19 not as a feature update, but within the larger picture of the future of the web as React sees it.
- I want to think together about the path React has taken and where it wants to go, and discuss whether we agree with that direction.
- CSR, SSR, and RSC are familiar interview topics, but I have not studied them deeply. I hope this can connect concepts I knew into a single flow.

1. Client-Side Rendering (CSR)

Web applications originally followed a model where the server generated HTML
and the browser displayed it. As applications became more complex, regenerating
an entire page on the server created problems:

- Even a small UI change required rendering the entire page again.
- More user interactions meant more round trips to the server.
- Keeping state on the client was difficult.

CSR emerged from a different idea: calculate UI on the client, not the
server.

 

 CSR is a method where the browser receives empty HTML such as
    and dynamically builds the whole UI through a
 JavaScript bundle.

1. The browser sends a request: GET /.
2. The server sends a simple HTML file and JavaScript file containing only the
   minimum structure (TTFB).

3. The browser downloads and renders HTML and CSS, creating the initial page
   structure. At this point, users see a blank page.
4. It downloads and executes JavaScript through the   tag. React and
   other libraries run, and the UI is created. The entire application is inside
   the JavaScript bundle.
5. JavaScript adds behavior to the HTML received from the server, making the
   page interactive.
6. The client calls APIs to fetch the data it needs.
7. The UI is completed from that data; this is when LCP is measured.

 

1. Initial loading speed

Only after HTML and CSS render can JavaScript be downloaded, parsed, and
executed; only then does the page become interactive. The problem is that every
step must happen in sequence: it is slow, and the user experience suffers.

2. JavaScript bundle size

CSR sends the whole application to the client. As features grow, so does the
JavaScript bundle, and the browser needs more time to process it—especially on
mobile.

3. SEO

Search engines primarily index the server-provided HTML, such as
  , which makes CSR content difficult to analyze. Without
a   tag, a CSR application can provide only an empty DOM structure.
Even though Googlebot can execute JavaScript, a limited crawl budget makes it
hard to collect all content from a complex SPA.

 Do we have to calculate all UI on the client?

 What if the server calculated the initial UI in advance?

2. Server-Side Rendering (SSR)

 SSR renders the page on the server and sends the browser complete HTML.

1. The browser requests GET / from the server.
2. The server generates HTML: fetch data → create the component tree → create
   HTML.
3. It sends completed HTML, already containing content, to the browser.
4. The browser downloads the JavaScript bundle: React runtime, application
   code, event handlers, and state logic.
5. When JavaScript runs, it hydrates the generated HTML.

Hydration connects JavaScript behavior to static HTML generated on the server
so that it becomes interactive. It creates a virtual DOM, compares it with the
server HTML, connects event handlers, and initializes application state.

 

1. SEO: Because the server provides full HTML, crawlers can index content
   more easily.
2. User experience: Unlike CSR, where users see a blank screen until
   JavaScript runs, SSR can show a completed page beforehand—though it is not
   interactive yet.

 

If the server already made the HTML, why does React not use it as-is? The
answer is the hydration invariant: React must ensure that server DOM equals the
client render output. If the HTML generated on the server and the result React
renders again on the client differ, there is a hydration mismatch.

When they differ, React cannot know which DOM is correct. During hydration, it
does not simply trust the HTML: it rebuilds the component tree. This is why SSR
still needs significant client computation.

 

SSR improved initial loading, but pre-React 18 SSR had structural problems.

1. The server had to fetch all required data before it could start rendering
HTML.

For a page that shows data from a database or another API, the server had to
produce complete HTML containing all that data: fetch required data → render
components from it → return complete HTML. The process was synchronous: one
step could not continue until the previous step finished.

2. All JavaScript had to be loaded before hydration could begin.

React did not hydrate a component tree in stages; it processed the whole tree
at once. If JavaScript logic was not ready for any part of the page, hydration
could not proceed. Since it ran to completion once started, everything had to
be ready first.

3. Every hydration task had to finish before components became interactive.

Once hydration began, React worked through the whole tree sequentially. It
could not pause midway or handle one component first. Hydration used major JavaScript
resources and blocked other JavaScript work, so users could not interact with
the application until it finished.

The core problem was hydrating the entire component tree at once. If one part
of an application rendered more slowly than another, this was very inefficient.
The React team considered rendering selected parts first and processing the
rest asynchronously. That led to Suspense.

3. React 18: Streaming SSR and Selective Hydration

Pre-React 18 SSR solved CSR's blank-screen problem fairly well. Because the
server sent complete HTML first, users could see page structure and content
earlier, and SEO was much better.

But showing HTML quickly and making UI interactive quickly are entirely
different problems. Pre-React 18 SSR improved the speed of what users could
see, but still had a structural bottleneck in the speed at which UI came alive.
Streaming SSR and Selective Hydration turn these three bottlenecks from one
large waterfall into smaller independent units.

 

Traditional SSR treated a page as one huge finished product. React 18 began to
see a page as a collection of regions with different readiness speeds and
priorities. The central idea that enables this shift is the Suspense boundary.

Suspense is often understood only as a way to show loading UI. In the context
of React 18 server rendering, it matters much more: it is a structural boundary
that can split server rendering and hydration. A boundary lets React treat
parts of a component tree as independent units.

- Some parts can be shown right now.
- Some parts do not have data or code ready yet.
- Show ready parts first.
- Attach the rest naturally when it is ready.

This is the starting point of Streaming SSR.

 

In traditional SSR, it was difficult for the server to begin responding before
the whole HTML document was finished. React 18 introduced streaming server
rendering. renderToPipeableStream sends HTML in chunks and sends ready parts
in sequence.

The server can send the shell—the initial skeleton that helps a user
understand the page—before everything is ready. onShellReady and
onAllReady support this flow.

Streaming SSR does not completely eliminate waterfalls in server rendering,
but it breaks them into smaller waterfalls. Users see page structure and
context rather than a state where nothing appears.

 

 Is showing HTML first enough?

What users want is not only a visible page but a page they can click and type
in. Streaming SSR reduces the server-response bottleneck, but major client-side
problems remain:

- JavaScript still has to download.
- React still has to hydrate.
- The point at which the whole page becomes interactive can still be late.

So Streaming SSR improves the speed of what users see, but does not
automatically solve the speed of becoming interactive. The other axis React
18 added is Selective Hydration.

 

Selective Hydration hydrates initial HTML in chunks, so one part of a page can
become interactive even while another part's code or data is not ready. Because
Suspense boundaries divide the tree into independent units, hydration can be
scheduled by importance.

Imagine a search input at the top of a page and a heavy recommendation list at
the bottom. In older SSR, a slow recommendation list or delayed code could also
delay the search input becoming interactive. With Selective Hydration, the
important input can hydrate first and the less important area later.

What matters is that Suspense is not merely “show a spinner while loading.” It
acts as a hydration scheduling boundary:

- This part can be handled independently.
- UI outside this boundary can appear and come alive first.
- Content inside the boundary can continue later once it is ready.

Suspense is therefore a structural split point for rendering and hydration.

 

Individually, these features can look like partial optimizations. Together,
they are one strategy for splitting both the server and client stages.

Streaming SSR solves:

- Not waiting for all HTML on the server to be ready.
- Showing ready UI structure first.

Selective Hydration solves:

- Not waiting for the whole tree on the client to come alive.
- Activating important interactions first.

React 18 changed server rendering from simply “making HTML on the server” into
an architecture that becomes visible progressively and interactive
progressively.

 

Streaming SSR and Selective Hydration were major improvements, but costs
remained.

1. The JavaScript bundle that the client must download is still the same.
   HTML can be sent asynchronously through streaming, but the browser must
   ultimately download the whole page's JavaScript. Does it have to?
2. There is still a cost to hydrate components that are not interactive.
   Not every UI needs the same level of client execution. Hydrating even static
   components seems like unnecessary resource use. Is there a way to avoid it?

4. RSC (React Server Components)

Streaming SSR and Selective Hydration made React server rendering much more
progressive. React could show ready parts before the whole HTML document was
finished, and make important parts interactive before the whole tree was ready.

But React 18 succeeded at splitting hydration into smaller pieces without
greatly reducing the total number of components that needed hydration. Read-only
Markdown, static content, data-heavy UI, and components that depend on
server-only data still went into the client bundle and became hydration
candidates. This is where RSC begins.

 

Server Components are a new kind of component rendered in an environment
separate from the client application or SSR server, before bundling. “Server”
does not necessarily mean a web server at request time: it can be a CI build
environment or a per-request server. The essence of RSC is not “make HTML on a
server,” but run components outside the client bundle.

 Do not send every component to the client. Keep components that only need to
 run on the server there.

 

- The payload contains rendered Server Component output, placeholders showing
  where Client Components belong, references to their JavaScript files, and
  props information.
- RSC is an architecture that uses HTML and an RSC Payload together.
- On initial load, HTML is a fast non-interactive preview; the RSC Payload then
  reconciles the server/client tree, and JavaScript for Client Components
  hydrates last.

 

That component can have zero client JavaScript.

- Database access does not enter the client bundle.
- Heavy work such as Markdown parsing does not go to the client.
- The component itself is not a hydration target.

 

Earlier approaches forced every component through hydration. With RSC, only
components needing interaction add "use client" and hydrate selectively.
Static content that needs no interaction does not go through hydration, so
resources are not wasted.

 

- Data can be fetched directly on the server, reducing server-client round
  trips.
- Sensitive data stays on the server and is not exposed to the client.
- In the App Router, an async Server Component can directly access a database
  or file system without a separate API endpoint.

 

1. Render Server Components on the server. React executes the Server
   Component tree and creates the special RSC Payload. Individual chunks can be
   split by route segment and Suspense boundary.
2. Generate HTML using the RSC Payload and Client Component instructions.
   Initial HTML remains important, but it reflects RSC output and Client
   Component references rather than only SSR output.
3. Use HTML first for a fast, non-interactive preview. This connects to SSR
   and Streaming SSR.
4. Use the RSC Payload to reconcile the server/client component tree. The
   payload updates the DOM and identifies where Client Components belong and
   what references they need.
5. Hydrate Client Component JavaScript last. Hydration does not disappear;
   it remains only for Client Components.

Thoughts

- React keeps offering increasingly sophisticated tools and strategies for
  maximizing performance.
- CSR → SSR → Streaming SSR → RSC are choices for faster, more efficient UX.
- But the technology becomes more complex too, and fully following the React
  team's context may itself become a development resource.
- In the paradox that “the code becomes more complex, but users get a simpler
  experience,” we need the ability to manage that complexity.
- Rather than adopting things blindly, it seems better to consider trade-offs
  and choose according to the situation.

 

- Since moving away from class components, React has continued to pursue more
  declarative and abstracted patterns—for example,
  useActionState,
  useFormStatus,
  and useOptimistic.
- It may become a competitive advantage not merely to use React's built-in
  features, but to make them our own and explain them in our own context.

title: Why Did React Leave Class Components Behind?
text:
1. In React, the Result Matters More Than the Process

React has pursued declarative UI from the beginning. What matters is not how
we arrive at a goal, but what we want to show. Under the philosophy that the
result matters more than the process, React has evolved toward hiding complex
procedures and expressing UI simply as the result of state.

Class components do not quite fit that philosophy. These two examples produce
the same UI, but the second asks readers to deal first with the process—a
render method and this binding.

Hooks arrived in React 16.8, marking a turning point in React's gradual move
from class components to function components. This article looks at some of
the reasons behind that shift.

2. Can You Trust this.state Three Seconds Later?

 Watch out for stale state!

 

Imagine a Counter that logs its count three seconds after a button click. If
you click it five times quickly, what should it log? We expect the value at
each click—1, 2, 3, 4, and 5—three seconds later.

But this class component does not behave that way:

Scenario

1. Click the button five times quickly → count = 5
2. Three seconds later, the console prints 5—always the latest value.

Why? A class component uses the this.state reference, which always points
to the latest state. To log 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 in a class-based
structure, we need a separate variable or must manually create a closure inside
the timeout callback.

 

By contrast, a function component captures a state snapshot in a closure for
each render.

Now it logs 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 as expected. The useEffect callback
seals the count value from the render in which it was created. Even when it
runs later, that value does not change, so it records the state from the
moment the button was clicked.

Class components have traditionally struggled with retrieving the wrong value
from timeouts. This subtle difference between classes and functions can create
serious bugs in timeouts, event listeners, and asynchronous calls.

 

When a function component really needs to read the latest state, as in the
class example, it can use useRef:

This satisfies both needs: a latest value and a snapshot.

3. In Class Components, Functions Are Left Out of Data Flow

 

React emphasizes one-way data flow: everything flows through props. That must
include functions as well as numbers and strings, otherwise the dependency
graph is incomplete.

Class methods, however, are permanently bound to an instance, so their
reference (identity) does not change. React Fiber can therefore incorrectly
decide that there is no dependency, leaving the function out of data flow.

 

Here, Parent passes a fetchData function to Child. The function depends
on state in Parent.

Although it looks fine, there is a major problem: fetchData is a class
method. It is tied to the instance's this, and React cannot tell that it
depends on state. The function itself does not change when state changes, so
the comparison in componentDidUpdate is always false:

The child cannot call fetchData again even if the parent's state changes.
To work around this, we have to pass query as another prop merely to compare
the difference, even though the child only needs this.props.fetchData. This
breaks component encapsulation and blurs concerns.

 - this.fetchData keeps the same reference as long as the class instance lives.
 - Even if query changes from react to vue, Child cannot notice it.

Dependency decisions use the question, “Did the reference change?” A class
method is data, but it is treated as an unchanging constant.

 

1. useCallback with a dependency array

The function reference updates when query changes, so the child's effect can
run again.

2. Separate concerns with a custom Hook

Child receives only the data result, preserving encapsulation and making
testing easier. This approach addresses SRP, performance, testing, and bug
reduction together. In React, we should not forget that a function is data
that can change too.

4. Class Lifecycles Focus on Timing Rather Than Intent

To run effects in class components, we work with three lifecycle methods:

- componentDidMount
- componentDidUpdate
- componentWillUnmount

Working directly with lifecycles organizes code around when and how
something runs, rather than the intent of what it should do.

The logic is scattered by timing, weakening separation of concerns and making
the code harder to trace and maintain:

- Fragmented logic: fetchData is called in three places.
- Risk of duplication or omission: missing cleanup creates a memory leak.
- Timing-dependent bugs: changing query while polling can cause a race condition.

With useEffect, a function component can keep related logic in one block:

5. Hooks Maximize Composition and Reusability

 

When Hooks arrived in React 16.8, one question came to mind first: “What if
state-management logic could be moved outside a component?” Custom Hooks made
that possible by turning logic into reusable modules.

- UI = assembling components
- Logic = assembling Hooks

 

The JSX of 2017 began with “with with with…”

Before Hooks, reusing shared logic in classes meant stacking Higher-Order
Components (HOCs) or Render Props.

- Deeper JSX: DevTools trees fill with Wrapper nodes.
- Harder tracing: the real render node is difficult to find at a glance.
- Type propagation problems: generic props are redefined at every layer.

Render Props have a different shape, but cause the same pain when nested:

 

Hooks flatten the tree by clearly separating logic into Hooks and UI into
JSX.

Hooks hide the question “when and where should I lift this logic?” inside the
Hook, leaving the component only with “what result should I show?” They also
accelerated the growth of a module ecosystem: their single-function form lowers
the barrier to packaging and publishing on npm, while tools such as Storybook
and CodeSandbox can visualize a Hook's result immediately, making sharing and
validation much faster.

6. Class Components Have No Future

 

 Technical debt is the interest paid when a design chosen for today's
 convenience later collides with new features and performance goals.

The React team pushed function components because the class structure itself
revealed structural limits when moving to the next stage.
