In short, classes are designed around object orientation and imperative timing.
Their timing, binding, and references are intertwined, which does not fit
React's newer strategies of splitting work into small pieces, interrupting it,
and assigning priorities.

 

1. startTransition()—priority-based state updates

startTransition separates work a user should feel immediately from work that
is expensive but not urgent.

The transition queue stores snapshots of units of work and resumes them when
the browser has time. With classes, we would need to tag each setState call
with priority, manage the batching queue ourselves, and add guards in several
places so this.state does not change halfway through.

It is possible, but it requires low-level APIs such as
unstablebatchedUpdates, preserving this binding, and manual queue
synchronization. The code grows, and it must be adjusted again when React
versions change.

2. Suspense for data—the fit with the throw-Promise pattern

Function components and Hooks can naturally use the pattern “throw a Promise
during rendering, then replace it with loading UI at a Suspense boundary.”

With a class, the corresponding code is spread across methods:

Fetching moves into componentDidMount, error handling into
componentDidCatch, and local state must switch among loading, error, and
success. The logic is spread across methods, and when Suspense and an Error
Boundary overlap, render order needs separate adjustment. There is no
“best practice” exclusively for classes.

 

1. They must be serializable. Server Components are transformed at compile
time into pure functions without dependencies, and their result—the React
Element tree—is serialized and sent as a JSON stream. Props and internal state
must be serializable and side-effect free. Class methods, getters, and private
fields cannot be serialized or lose their meaning, leaving the compiler unable
to guarantee safety.

2. Re-entry must be safe. Streaming SSR sends HTML chunks, then continues
when data or CPU becomes available. The Fiber Scheduler stores snapshots of the
work stack.

 

In the end, class code either returns to an approach that streams only after a
whole page is complete, or is isolated for client-side use. It cannot fully
benefit from the faster LCP and INP offered by Streaming SSR.

 

- Concurrent Renderer, Server Components, and the Compiler are designed around functional assumptions.
- The cost in people, performance, and quality of building class-only workarounds rises quickly.
- Libraries, tools, and learning materials continue to accumulate around function components as the default.

So “class components have no future” does not mean they are impossible. It
means they carry a structural debt: every new feature requires another
compatibility workaround. There are only two choices:

1. Maintain the older design while absorbing an ever-growing compatibility layer.
2. Pay the one-time migration cost and move to a codebase where future features are the default.

Because the cost of building a “class compatibility adapter” for every new
feature is more expensive than the initial investment in function components,
the React community and most companies have already chosen the second path.

title: Is Class State Unpredictable? Try Immutable Objects
text:
TL;DR

- Objects are self-responsible entities. OOP design structures them like an ecosystem, where small objects collaborate to create larger capabilities.
- Good object design reveals responsibility through names. Object names should be nouns that express responsibility and identity, avoiding instrumental labels such as -er. Methods should distinguish between noun-like builders that return new objects and verb-like manipulators that change state. Treat side-effect-free values like properties, but make state changes or external effects explicit as methods.
- An object's identifier is an immutable coordinate that distinguishes it in the world and preserves its identity, so it should be encapsulated from external change. When objects have the same state, they can be treated as having the same meaning even if they are different instances in memory, improving predictability, testability, cache efficiency, and concurrency safety.
- Design objects to be immutable whenever possible: return new objects rather than changing state, for greater predictability, concurrency safety, and simplicity. A faithful object does not change itself, but models the world honestly by reflecting changes in the external entity through the same identifier. Unlike constant objects, whose state is their identifier, mutable objects need a separate identifier to preserve their identity.
- Good collaboration begins with depending on contracts rather than implementations. Interfaces are the rules of an object society, reducing coupling and allowing the system to evolve.

1. Respecting Objects Starts with Naming Them Carefully

 

Object-oriented design is ultimately a language of respect. An object is not
just a data structure. It is a responsible participant: we entrust it with
work, expect something from it, and ask it to collaborate with other objects.

The first thing we can do as designers is give an object a name worthy of that
role. Its name should reveal its responsibility and identity. We should be able
to look at the name and understand who the object is and what role it plays.

An object's name comes before the object itself. It is more than an explanation
for the client that uses it; it also reveals the designer's attitude and how
the designer understands the object.

 

Adding -er to a class name can reduce an object to a utility that works for
someone else:

The same idea leads to names such as:

- UserRegisterer → Registration
- Manager → Project
- Sender → Message

The -er suffix can turn an object into a wrapper around a helper function
without revealing its identity or responsibility. An object should not merely
assist another object. It should own a responsibility and act on its own.

 

Class names are not the only names that matter. Our understanding of an object
also appears in its method names.

Methods can be divided into two broad categories:

 
   
    Builder

    - creates or transforms something and returns a new object,
    - always has a return value,
    - does not change internal state, and
    - uses a name that describes the resulting object.

   
   
    typescript
    class Book {
      withAuthor(author: string): Book {}
      withTitle(title: string): Book {}
    }

    const book1 = new Book();
    const book2 = book1.withTitle("The Elegant Object");
    const book3 = book2.withAuthor("Yegor Bugayenko");
    

    book1 does not change. Each builder returns a new object, preserving
    immutability while allowing objects to be composed.

   
 

 
   
    Manipulator

    - changes an entity or some state in the real world,
    - returns no value,
    - uses a verb, such as save, put, remove, or quicklyPrint, and
    - makes the state-changing action clear.

   
   
    typescript
    printer.save();
    printer.quicklyPrint();
    printer.remove("trash.txt");
    

    The action itself is the manipulator's responsibility.

   
 

 

CQS stands for Command–Query Separation.

 A method that changes state—a command—should not return a value. A method that
 returns a value—a query—should not change state.

In other words, one method should have one responsibility.

- saveAndReturnId() saves state and returns a value at the same time.
- updateAndLog() combines a change with another side effect.

 

Some methods feel as though they could be properties:

From the outside, it does not matter whether a value was calculated or stored.
If it represents an attribute, it can look like a property.

- A simple attribute can be exposed as a property.
- A computed value can use a getter if reading it has no side effects.
- If reading the value changes something internally or affects the outside
  world, method syntax should make that behavior explicit.

 

- A class name should reveal an object's identity and responsibility.
- Avoid -er where it reduces an object to a tool; prefer a noun that
  represents its role.
- Distinguish builders from manipulators.
- Give each method one responsibility through CQS.
- Treat information that behaves like an attribute as an attribute, but make
  side effects explicit with method syntax.

 
  Must an immutable object's builder always have a noun-like name? How can we
  choose builder names that clearly describe the new object they return?
 

2. An Object's Identifier Is Its Coordinate in the World

An object is not just a collection of state. It needs a meaningful position,
and that position is its identifier.

 

An identifier distinguishes an object from the rest of the world. Its stability
allows the object to remain the same object over time. It acts like a
coordinate, an identity, or an address.

Consider a person. Their home address can change, but their government-issued
identifier does not. Whether they live in Seoul or Gwangju, they remain the
same person. The address is state; the identifier preserves identity.

 

An identifier gives an object continuity. If the identifier changes, the object
becomes another object.

The identifier should therefore be immutable. At least the state that defines
the object's identity should not be changeable from outside. This is where
encapsulation matters.

Private fields provide one way to encapsulate state:

A closure can provide the same kind of boundary:

 

name1 and name2 are different instances in memory. If their state is
identical, however, we can regard them as logically equal objects.

Equality is a human concept. Two things do not need to be physically identical
if they carry the same meaning. Treating equal states as equal values can:

- improve predictability,
- remove unnecessary conditional branches,
- simplify tests, and
- make caching and comparison easier.

An object should have a stable identity, and that identity should not change.
When identity becomes unstable, the object becomes unstable too.

 
  Shared mutable state is the central problem in concurrent environments.
  Multiple threads reading or changing one object can conflict, requiring
  synchronization through locks or mutexes. An immutable object never changes
  internally, so several threads can access it without observing a partial
  mutation.
 

3. Prefer Immutable Objects and Delay Mutability

 An immutable object cannot modify itself in any way. It must create and return
 a new object with the desired state.

The world itself is mutable. Addresses, bank balances, and even moods change.
That does not mean we cannot model the world with immutable objects. Immutable
objects shift our attention from what was mutated to how the state before
and after the change differs.

 

Several benefits are visible even in this small example.

Predictability

- five never changes.
- fifty is a completely different object.
- the two values do not unexpectedly share changing state.

No bugs caused by observing a partial mutation

A mutable object can expose an intermediate state:

If an asynchronous interruption occurs between the assignments, another part
of the program may observe only half of the update. Once an object mutates,
programmers must track which line runs first and which line must follow it.

Immutable objects avoid this problem because they never enter a partially
mutated state.

Smaller objects

An immutable object can initialize its state only when it is created. If a
constructor keeps growing, that pressure can reveal that the class owns too
many responsibilities and should be divided. The resulting objects tend to be
smaller and clearer.

 

Working with immutable objects naturally encourages a style similar to pure
functions:

- input becomes output,
- side effects are avoided, and
- state is not shared through mutation.

OOP and FP are different paradigms, but both aim for predictable code and
separated complexity.

 
   
    OOP

    Objects own responsibilities and collaborate. Complexity is managed by
    separating responsibilities across objects.

   
   
    FP

    Functions transform data without changing state. Predictability comes from
    calculations without side effects.

   
 

Immutable OOP can therefore converge toward an object-design philosophy that is
close to pure functions.

 

Is this WebPage immutable or mutable?

The uri cannot change, and the object's structure remains the same. The result
of content(), however, depends on the web server and network.

The object can still be understood as a faithful object:

- it always refers to the same URI, and
- it faithfully reflects the current state of the real web page at that URI.

The object itself does not change, but the world it represents can change, so
its behavior can return a different result.

 An immutable object does not change itself, but it can faithfully respond to
 changes in the entity it represents.

 

An object consists of an identifier, state, and behavior:

- Identifier — the reference, coordinate, or path that distinguishes it.
- State — the current state of the entity it represents.
- Behavior — the logic it performs when it receives a message.

For WebPage:

- the identifier is uri,
- the state is the page's current content, and
- the behavior is reading that state through content().

The important point is that the object itself has not changed.

 

A constant object has the same state and identifier. Name("Hwanhee", "Jung")
and Point(3, 4) are examples: their state is their identity, and neither
changes.

- Constant object — Its state is its identity. Both its meaning and content
  remain unchanged.
- Faithful object — The object is immutable, but it faithfully reflects
  changes in the external entity it represents.
- Mutable object — Its internal state can change, so it needs a separate
  identifier to preserve its identity over time.

Every constant object is immutable, but not every immutable object is constant.

4. Objects Collaborate, and Collaboration Needs Contracts

The central keyword in object-oriented design is collaboration.

 

An object eventually encounters work it cannot perform alone. It uses, calls,
or depends on another object.

Dependencies have different strengths:

- Tight coupling connects objects directly.
- Loose coupling lets objects collaborate while knowing less about one
  another.

Tight coupling may not look harmful at first. As a project grows, however,
strongly connected objects make testing, refactoring, and change more
difficult.

 

Objects perform responsibilities inside an environment. That environment is
social: relationships and collaboration are unavoidable.

The important question is not whether objects collaborate, but how tightly they
are coupled. Strong coupling makes tests harder, complicates refactoring, and
allows one change to spread like a domino effect.

We cannot remove collaboration, so we need a buffer between collaborators.

 

 An interface is a contract that an object follows in order to collaborate
 with another object.

An object only needs to know the interface. It does not need to know how the
other object implements that contract.

The interface states that any Cash must provide
multiply(factor: number): Cash.

DefaultCash declares that it follows the Cash contract.

Employee does not need to know the concrete DefaultCash implementation. It
trusts only the contract that a Cash provides multiply.

 

TypeScript supports multiple interfaces, allowing one class to fulfill several
roles:

 

A public method is a point of contact with other objects. If public methods are
added without a contract or clear intention:

- callers may use them in unintended ways,
- teams cannot tell which methods are stable and which are internal,
- external code can become dependent on implementation details, and
- every object can develop a different usage pattern.

Interfaces make those collaborative expectations explicit and help preserve a
consistent design.

5. Unanswered Questions

Many questions remain unresolved.

 

If every change returns a new object, does the design become too expensive in
memory or performance? Is continuously allocating objects always the right
tradeoff? The practical question is which approach remains easier to maintain.

 

Why not allow several threads to update the UI if multithreading can be faster?
Multiple threads trying to change the screen at the same time create races and
can leave the UI inconsistent during an interaction. Locks, queues, or
transactions would then be needed to coordinate every update.

For a UI, consistency is often more important than parallel mutation. Even
React's Virtual DOM comparison has its own cost, so the tradeoff is not simply
single-threaded versus fast.

 

Imperative code still runs somewhere underneath a declarative API. Is it
meaningful to say that we have made the code declarative merely by wrapping
that implementation? The important question may be where and how we design the
boundary.

 

OOP and FP can look like opposites. The more I study them, however, the more
they seem to pursue similar goals in different languages.

Other questions remain:

- Where should we draw the line between getters and methods?
- How should we model time and events if objects are truly collaborating
  participants?
- In frontend code, is a user interaction a command or a message?

title: Is an Invisible Side Effect Harmless?
text:
1. Is an Invisible Side Effect Harmless?

 If a tree falls in the forest, but no one is around to hear it, does it still
 make a sound?

It sounds like a philosophical question, but it maps surprisingly well to
programming: if a side effect occurs and no one observes it, is it still a
problem?

Avoiding side effects is a common goal in software design. Functional
programming takes that idea further by favoring pure functions—functions that
return the same output for the same input without changing external state.

In practice, though, side effects are unavoidable. Fetching data and managing a
cache are two obvious examples. We minimize them not because all side effects
are inherently bad, but because fewer side effects make code easier to reason
about.

A function that silently changes external state may look pure when nothing
currently reads that state. But the side effect is still there.

As soon as another part of the program starts reading the changed state, this
can lead to an unexpected bug. If the result also depends on call order, the
function becomes harder to test and understand.

To see why, let us start with referential transparency and the value of pure
functions.

2. Referential Transparency and Pure Functions

A pure function generally satisfies two conditions:

- It produces no side effects.
- It always returns the same output for the same input.

Purity is closely related to referential transparency.

 
  An expression is referentially transparent when replacing it with its
  resulting value does not change the program's behavior.
 

If f(x) evaluates to y, replacing f(x) with y should not change the
program's behavior.

Here, avg stores the result of calculateAverage(numbers). Replacing the
function call with that result produces the same behavior:

The output does not change, so calculateAverage(numbers) is referentially
transparent.

A referentially transparent expression can be treated like a value. Once we
know that calculateAverage(numbers) returns 9, we do not need to trace the
function again every time it appears.

That is the practical value of referential transparency: it lowers cognitive
load by letting us understand each expression in isolation.

3. The Risk of Hidden Side Effects

 

Consider a slightly different implementation:

Every call resets sum to zero and returns 9, so the function appears pure.
But it still has a hidden side effect:

- sum is declared outside the function.
- calculateAverage mutates that external variable.
- No other code currently reads sum, so the mutation is not visible.

The side effect has not disappeared. It is simply unobserved.

 

calculateAverage(numbers) returns the same value for the same input. In this
program, replacing the call with 9 also seems safe because nothing else reads
sum.

The expression looks referentially transparent in this context, but the
function is still impure. Its side effect just happens to be invisible—for now.

 

A hidden side effect may seem harmless in a small program. As the codebase
grows, however, it creates several risks:

- A maintenance change can suddenly make the side effect observable.
- The function no longer behaves independently.
- The program becomes harder to predict.

At first, nothing else uses the global sum. A later function might:

After calculateAverage runs, sum still holds the accumulated total.
calculateSum adds to that existing value and returns the wrong result. A
previously invisible side effect now changes the program's behavior.

A reader may not immediately notice that sum is external. Making it local
removes that ambiguity:

Now sum belongs to the function, and calculateAverage no longer mutates
external state.

 

A side effect is not safe just because no one observes it today. Hidden effects
make code harder to maintain and can surface as bugs when the surrounding code
changes.

Pure, referentially transparent functions do not depend on a hidden execution
history. That makes them easier to read, test, and reuse.

4. Side Effects for Performance

Sometimes we introduce side effects deliberately for performance. Caching and
memoization trade internal state for less repeated work. The question is how to
make that trade without giving up predictability.

 

The first call to specialNumber(n) computes a value. Later calls reuse the
cached result. But this implementation also hides a side effect:

- It mutates the global cache.
- The function does not reveal that it changes external state.
- Other code can change or reset the cache.

Because external code can reset the cache, callers cannot know whether the next
call will hit the cache or recompute the value:

 

A closure keeps the mutable state private and prevents unrelated code from
changing it directly:

The cache is still mutable, but the rest of the program cannot access it. From a
caller's perspective, the function still returns the same output for the same
input.

When an optimization needs state, keep that state as local as possible.

5. Managing Side Effects Safely

We cannot always remove side effects, but we can make them explicit,
predictable, and controlled.

 

Start by separating pure data transformation from the code that performs the
effect:

calculateTax is pure and easy to test. printTax has a side effect, but its
name and responsibility make that clear. The effect is visible at the call
site instead of being buried inside the calculation.

 

Another option is to return the data an effect needs instead of performing the
effect immediately:

createLogMessage stays pure and independently testable. console.log happens
explicitly at the program boundary.

 

Functional programming can represent an effect as work to run later. An IO
monad, for example, delays the operation until the program explicitly executes
it:

A test can verify the planned effect without triggering console.log. The
effect still exists, but executing it becomes an explicit decision.

 

React's useEffect follows a similar principle: it moves side effects out of
rendering and into a dedicated lifecycle. It does not eliminate effects, but it
does give them a visible boundary and a predictable place to run.

6. Visibility Matters More Than Disappearance

 If a tree falls in the forest, but no one is around to hear it, does it still
 make a sound?

Hiding a side effect does not make it harmless. The best option is to design
the code so that the effect cannot occur in the first place.

When an effect is unavoidable, separate it from pure logic, keep mutable state
as local as possible, and make the execution point explicit. The goal is not
to hide side effects, but to make them predictable and controllable.

title: Building a Type-Safe Pipe Function
text:
1. Introducing pipe

After building a curry utility, I wanted to build pipe. A pipe function runs
several functions sequentially from left to right. That makes a transformation
flow visible in the code and fits naturally with declarative programming.

The result of add becomes the input to multiply, and then to subtract. The flow
is correct, but it has to be read from the inside out.

With pipe, the same work reads in execution order:

The sequence add → multiply → subtract is visible at a glance. Rather than
describing how to nest calls, the code describes what transformations make
up the operation.

2. Two Shapes for pipe

 

Pipe utilities usually take one of two forms:

The first is an immediate-execution style, used by
fp-ts. Because
the value is supplied first, calling pipe evaluates the chain immediately.

The second is a curried style, used by libraries such as
Ramda:

Here, pipe returns a new function. Defining transformations before supplying
data makes function composition itself the first-class operation. This is the
form I chose to implement.

3. Type-Safe Composition in TypeScript

 

A typed pipe needs to guarantee two things:

- Each function's return type matches the next function's input type.
- The pipe's final return type is the return type of its last function.

Given (arg: X) = Y, (arg: Y) = Z, and (arg: Z) = K, the argument of function
n + 1 must be the return type of function n.

 

My first thought was to describe the whole chain recursively. The article
How to use advanced TypeScript to define a pipe function
takes this approach:

Its advantage is clear: a pipe can accept an unlimited number of functions.
But that flexibility comes with a more complicated type system and can slow type
checking as chains grow.

 

A pipe with ten or more functions is rarely easier to understand. Long chains
are often better expressed as meaningful intermediate steps:

Breaking a long sequence apart gives transformations names and makes the logic
easier to inspect. It also avoids asking the TypeScript checker to recursively
follow an arbitrarily long chain.

 

Function overloading gives one function several call signatures—each with its
own parameter and return types—while keeping one runtime implementation:

The same technique is a good fit for pipe. Each overload describes one allowed
chain length and ensures that adjacent functions connect correctly:

In practice, I would continue the overload signatures to a sensible maximum,
such as ten functions. That gives the editor precise inference and clear error
messages without introducing a deeply recursive type.

4. Closing Thoughts

I started by considering a recursive type system that would support unlimited
function chains. But three constraints mattered more:

- The types become difficult to understand.
- Compile-time performance can deteriorate.
- Pipes longer than ten functions are uncommon and often deserve to be split.

For this utility, overloads are the better engineering tradeoff. They are
explicit, fast, easy to maintain, and still cover the practical cases.

Sometimes the less clever solution is the more useful one. TypeScript's type
system is powerful, but code should still be guided by the readability and
usage patterns that people actually encounter.

 

fp-ts reaches
the same conclusion for its own pipe implementation.

title: Building a Type-Safe Curry Function
text:
0. Functional Programming and Currying

While studying functional programming, I came across currying. At first, it
looked like little more than a technique for breaking a complex function into
smaller ones. The further I followed it, however, the more it seemed to capture
several ideas at the heart of functional programming.

 

Functional programming tends to emphasize:

- functions as first-class values,
- immutability,
- pure functions,
- declarative programming,
- composition and modularity, and
- higher levels of abstraction.

Together, these principles model a program as a flow of data and
transformations.

 

Currying transforms a function of N arguments into a sequence of N functions,
each accepting one argument. The name comes from the mathematician Haskell
Curry.

add receives both arguments at once. curriedAdd receives a, returns
another function, and lets that function receive b.

 

Functions become values

A curried function returns another function, making first-class functions
visible in everyday code:

double is a reusable value produced from a more general function.

Immutability and pure functions remain natural

Partial application creates a new function without modifying the original one.
Each step returns a value rather than mutating external state.

Composition and reuse become easier

Currying produces unary functions that fit naturally into composition:

add3 fixes one argument of add, producing a smaller function with a clearer
purpose.

General operations can become specific tools

filterBy is a reusable higher-order function. Partial application turns it
into filterEven, a function that expresses one concrete operation.

Intent becomes more declarative

greaterThan(10) describes what qualifies. filterBy handles how the array
is traversed.

Many functional utility libraries provide curry as a foundation. Looking at
the implementation in Rambda left me with a question: what would it take to
build the same flexibility with useful TypeScript inference?

That made curry a good TypeScript exercise.

1. Defining the Curry Function

 

There are two common calling styles:

- Strict curry accepts exactly one argument at each step.
- Loose curry accepts one or more arguments at each step.

Haskell is designed around functional programming, and all of its functions are
curried by default. Even a function that appears to accept several arguments
behaves as a chain of unary functions:

add 3 returns a function that remembers x = 3; add3 5 supplies the second
argument. The syntax permits add 3 5, but the model remains a sequence of
single-argument applications.

That consistency makes behavior predictable and composition natural. In
JavaScript, though, forcing every caller to use nested single-argument calls can
be inconvenient. Loose currying preserves partial application while allowing a
more practical calling style, so that is what I chose to build:

 

The runtime design is simple: collect arguments until there are enough to call
the original function. Otherwise, return another curried function and continue
recursively.

The variables have distinct roles:

- collectedArgs contains arguments from earlier calls.
- newArgs contains arguments supplied by the current call.
- allArgs combines both groups.

isComplete compares the number of collected arguments with fn.length. When
there are enough, the original function runs. Otherwise, curry returns
another function and keeps collecting.

 

AnyFunc is a convenient unconstrained function type:

Parameters  extracts a function's arguments as a tuple:

At first, Partial  looks like a good model for
collectedArgs, because a curried call may have supplied only some parameters:

That gets the runtime structure working, but the function is still not type
safe.

2. Making the Input Generic

 

The first implementation accepts every value:

TypeScript should reject the string, but every argument has already widened to
any.

 

Making the input function generic allows the implementation to retain its
parameter tuple:

Now collectedArgs is constrained by the parameters of the specific Fn
passed to curry.

3. Partial Tuples and Rest Parameters

 

Typing collectedArgs as Partial  exposes another problem:

Conceptually, Partial makes each tuple position optional:

For a rest parameter, however, TypeScript needs a type it can confidently treat
as an array or tuple. I wanted an explicit tuple transformation that preserved
both ordering and optional positions.

 

The target behavior is:

Ordering matters here for more than satisfying the rest parameter. Currying
applies parameters from left to right. A caller may stop after any prefix, but
should not skip earlier positions and supply a later one in isolation:

PartialTuple recursively moves values from Params into an accumulator,
marking each position as optional:

Applied to the implementation:

The rest-parameter error disappears, and invalid parameter order can be
rejected at the type level.

 

The four generic names describe the recursion:

- Params: parameters still waiting to be processed.
- Accumulated: parameters already converted.
- CurrentParam: the first parameter in the current step.
- RemainingParams: every parameter after it.

 
   A closer look at each recursive step 
   
    The initial call splits [number, string, boolean] into number and
    [string, boolean], then appends number? to the accumulator.

    typescript
    PartialTuple 
    

    The second step extracts string and appends string?.

    typescript
    PartialTuple 
    

    The third step extracts boolean.

    typescript
    PartialTuple 
    

    An empty Params tuple reaches the base case and returns the accumulated
    optional tuple.

   
 

 
   The TypeScript syntax behind PartialTuple 
   
    Conditional types

    extends checks whether a type matches a constraint:

    typescript
    type Check  = T extends string ? "Yes" : "No";

    type Result1 = Check ; // "Yes"
    type Result2 = Check ; // "No"
    

    Pattern matching with infer

    Within a conditional type, infer captures part of the matched structure:

    typescript
    type UnpackArray  = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T;

    type Result1 = UnpackArray ; // number
    type Result2 = UnpackArray ; // string
    

    In Params extends [infer CurrentParam, ...infer RemainingParams],
    TypeScript captures the first tuple item as CurrentParam and the rest as
    RemainingParams. The [Head, ...Tail] pattern also ensures that the tuple
    contains at least one element before the recursive branch runs.

   
 

4. Requiring at Least One Argument

 

Currying is useful because it partially applies an original function. A call
that supplies no arguments makes no progress:

This can be prevented before runtime.

 

AtLeastOneParam keeps the first parameter required and makes every remaining
position optional:

If Fn takes no arguments, the type resolves to never and prevents a curried
call. Otherwise:

This shape supports loose partial application while guaranteeing that every
call contributes at least one value.

5. Deriving the Curried Return Type

The runtime function is ready, but its return type still needs to describe two
different outcomes:

1. If parameters remain, return another curried function.
2. If every parameter has been supplied, return the original result.

 

First, RemainingParameters removes one expected parameter for each applied
argument:

For example:

The recursion consumes both tuples in parallel. When there are no applied
arguments left, the remaining expected tuple is the answer.

 

CurriedFunction uses that remaining tuple to decide what the next call
returns:

AppliedParams must contain at least one valid parameter. If
RemainingParameters contains at least one element, the return value is another
CurriedFunction whose input is the remaining tuple. When nothing remains, the
return value becomes ReturnType .

The implementation can now declare the complete return type:

6. The Finished API

The final type supports flexible grouping without losing parameter order,
argument types, or the original return type:

The runtime behavior was the easy part: collect arguments and recurse until
fn.length is satisfied. The real work was expressing the same state machine
in the type system.

Recursive tuple types turned out to be a natural fit. PartialTuple models the
prefix collected so far, AtLeastOneParam guarantees progress on every call,
and RemainingParameters determines whether the next value should be another
function or the final result.

The complete implementation is also available in the
function-al project.

title: Thinking in Graph
text:
1. From a RESTful Mindset to GraphQL

A few days ago, I came across an interview with Lenz, a maintainer of Apollo
Client. I opened it hoping to hear the story behind Suspense support in Apollo
Client. Instead, something from the opening discussion stayed with me: the
interviewer described how surprising GraphQL felt when it first appeared inside
a large organization.

That story is a useful place to begin.

 
   
   Interview with Lenz, an Apollo Client maintainer. 
 

The interviewer first encountered GraphQL around 2015 while working at IBM.
Across the company, many teams owned different sets of data, and their systems
communicated through REST APIs. The arrangement sounds straightforward, but at
that scale it created a surprising number of problems.

 

1. Inconsistent contracts

Each team created its own endpoints and returned data shaped around individual
requests. There was no strong guarantee that separate teams would expose data
consistently or use compatible response formats. Consumers ended up writing
substantial amounts of code to normalize and combine those responses.

2. No single source of truth

As teams added more request-specific endpoints, the same data appeared in
several places. Without a reliable source of truth, teams had to keep talking to
one another simply to track changes elsewhere in the organization.

3. Excessive coordination

Every team needed to announce data changes and create new endpoints when another
team needed a different shape. That coordination became a serious drag on
developer productivity.

 “I think that's a really big challenge in code because codebases are too big
 for everybody to keep full context.”

4. Endpoint sprawl

To reduce repeated conversations, teams often responded to requests by creating
another custom endpoint:

 Frontend: “We need this data.”

The result was more duplication, more endpoint-specific logic, and an API that
became increasingly difficult to keep consistent.

 

GraphQL approached the problem differently: define the required data explicitly
and fetch only that data. Unlike a REST API, where the server fixes the shape of
each endpoint, GraphQL lets the client describe the shape of the response.

Even someone seeing GraphQL for the first time can read this query and infer
that the client needs a user's name, email, and post titles. There is no reason
to fetch unrelated fields or add another endpoint just for this view.

 

1. Flexible data requests

GraphQL clients can select the fields they need for each use case while REST endpoints return a predefined response.

2. Schema-driven design

A GraphQL schema makes the API's data structures and relationships explicit.
Teams only need to share the relevant contract. A team that owns user data, for
example, can expose that a User has an id without revealing its internal
implementation. The schema itself gives clients enough information to explore
the data model without maintaining a separate, always-outdated API guide.

3. Field-level usage analysis

Because GraphQL records requests at the field level, a team can see which fields
are frequently used. If an expensive field has no consumers, deprecating it
becomes a much safer decision.

4. Predictable caching and data integrity

Explicit response shapes also make client-side caching easier. Apollo Client,
for example, can normalize entities and remove duplicate data automatically.

A REST mutation can return updated data too, but clients often issue a separate
refetch to restore confidence that local state is current. GraphQL mutations are
commonly designed to return the changed entity, allowing the client to merge
that result directly into its normalized cache.

2. I Had Been Using GraphQL Like REST

 

As I worked with GraphQL, I realized that I had never fully left the RESTful
mindset behind. It showed most clearly in the names and structure of my schema.
The difference became obvious during a refactor.

 
   
    
   
   
    
   
 

Names such as getAlbum and getAlbumTracks read like REST endpoint names.
They describe an operation—get this resource—and focus attention on the act of
fetching.

GraphQL, however, is built around a graph. A graph consists of nodes and edges.
Nodes represent entities such as Album and Track; edges represent the
relationships between them, such as Album → Tracks.

Schema design should reflect that model. Instead of asking “What should I
fetch?”, the better question is Which nodes and relationships should the client
be able to traverse?

I renamed getAlbum and getSavedAlbums to album and savedAlbums. The new
names describe nodes rather than commands.

A GraphQL query does not merely retrieve data. It traverses relationships:

This query begins at an album node and follows the graph through its tracks to
each track's artist. The relationships are visible directly in the shape of the
query.

With a RESTful approach, the same traversal could require several endpoint
calls:

 

It is worth checking whether a schema exposes several queries for the same node
type:

Here, the schema defines two query fields for the same User node: one lookup
by ID and another by name. This is a common way to reproduce REST endpoint
design inside GraphQL.

It creates three problems:

1. The schema is organized around operations rather than nodes.
2. Each additional query can duplicate resolver logic on the server.
3. Every new lookup condition requires yet another query field.

A single query with filter arguments is more flexible:

The schema now has one entry point for the User node. New lookup conditions
can be added as arguments instead of creating a growing list of operation-like
queries.

Where REST might expose both GET /users/:id and
GET /users?name=Alice, GraphQL can handle both requests through the same
user field.

3. GraphQL Data Is a Graph

 

Resolver chaining means that resolvers work as a connected sequence: the result
of one resolver becomes the parent input of another. A player resolver can
return currentTrack, and the resolver for CurrentTrack can supply lyrics
only when the client asks for that field.

 

1. Resolve the player query

The player resolver requests the currently playing track and queue from the
Spotify API, maps the response into PlayerState, and returns currentTrack as
a CurrentTrack.

2. Resolve the lyrics field

The returned currentTrack becomes the parent value for the CurrentTrack
resolver. If the query includes lyrics, that field resolver fetches the lyric
data and returns a Lyrics value.

Each field can have an independent resolver, and GraphQL executes the work
needed for the fields selected by the client.

 

1. Unrequested data requires no work

GraphQL invokes field resolvers according to the client's selection set. If the
client does not request lyrics, the CurrentTrack.lyrics resolver does not
run. That avoids unnecessary resource usage.

2. Requests remain flexible

Clients can omit lyrics when a screen does not need it, reducing both server
work and network payload size.

3. Resolver ownership stays local

Each field is managed independently. Changing the implementation of one field
does not require rewriting unrelated resolvers, which improves maintainability
and makes the schema easier to extend.

4. Relationships are visible

The path player → currentTrack → lyrics makes the relationship between the
data explicit in both the schema and the query. That is GraphQL's graph-based
model in practice.

4. A Mid-Project Reflection

 

My project does not contain enough data yet for GraphQL's advantages to feel
dramatic. I have experimented with resolver chaining, field-based design, and
other GraphQL concepts, but their impact is still difficult to measure. That
may partly reflect gaps in my own understanding.

The ideal path for adopting a technique would look like this:

1. The application is slow.
2. Investigation shows that it requests unnecessary data.
3. I separate the work through resolver chaining.
4. The unnecessary requests disappear and performance improves.

My actual path has been closer to this:

1. I want to use GraphQL effectively.
2. I discover resolver chaining.
3. I look for somewhere to apply it.
4. I implement it, but cannot yet feel a meaningful difference.

That second path starts with a technology rather than a problem. Recognizing
that difference made me realize that I still have work to do before I can use
GraphQL with real depth.

 

GraphQL is not simply a replacement for an API style. It is a design philosophy
centered on exploring data and expressing relationships. Its value grows with
the size of a project and the complexity of its data.

My current project has a relatively small and simple data model. GraphQL's
advantages would be easier to see in a system where:

- several teams independently own parts of the same data graph,
- relationships between entities are complex,
- clients query the same nodes through many combinations of conditions, or
- large requests make caching and performance optimization important.

A toy project gives me room to learn these ideas, but not always enough
pressure to prove why they matter.

 

1. Use GraphQL to solve problems

I want to begin with an observed problem rather than stopping at the act of
adopting a tool:

- Repeated field selections → introduce fragments.
- Several teams own different parts of one graph → explore Federation so each
  team can work independently.

2. Build a TypeScript integration that fits the project

I am still considering how GraphQL and TypeScript should work together. Custom
hooks do not fit every React Server Components use case, while GraphQL Code
Generator may provide a better foundation. I want to examine the tradeoffs
carefully and develop a repeatable practice of my own.

3. Experience GraphQL in large-scale collaboration

I would like to experience the problems GraphQL was designed to address:

- letting teams own data independently and composing it through Federation,
- collaborating on schema design and integration, and
- designing caching strategies for complex, high-volume data.

5. Closing Thoughts

GraphQL feels more like a philosophy for exploring data and designing relationships rather than a mechanism for sending requests and receiving responses.
Its benefits will naturally feel different depending on the scale and complexity of the
system around it.

Over the last few days, I have spent a great deal of energy trying to use
GraphQL well inside a small project. Not every feature produces a visible
payoff yet. Even so, learning to see data as nodes and relationships feels
valuable in its own right. Each attempt to understand that design philosophy is
practice for the larger systems—and larger teams—where those choices carry much
more weight.

Feature releases and experiments were spread across client code, deployments, internal documents, Slack conversations, and individual memory. What first looked like separate operational inconveniences was one fragmented workflow.

By observing how the team actually worked, I connected release control, experiment context, and lifecycle monitoring as parts of the same system. I initiated the project and led it from problem discovery through implementation.

01. Identifying Problems

I traced recurring moments of friction back through the workflow, then tested whether they were isolated requests or symptoms of the same system.

 

A. Slow shutdown

- No targeted shutdown — Disabling one feature still required a code change, build, deployment, and verification.
- Unsafe rollback — Reverting the deployment also removed unrelated, healthy features shipped alongside it.

B. Manual experiments

- Engineer-dependent QA — Testing another variant required database access, account changes, or help from an engineer.
- Deployment-bound operations — Rollout and variant changes repeatedly created avoidable deployments.
- Frequent context switching — Small requests interrupted engineering work and reduced focus.

C. Missed checkpoints

- Delayed validation — Instrumentation checks happened only when an engineer remembered them.
- Reactive analysis — Results were prepared after someone requested them, sometimes too late for a meeting.
- Lost context — Each analysis required the team to reconstruct decisions scattered across memory and documents.

 

I reviewed three years of deployment history to measure how much recurring work came from experiment operations.

 
   

    - 5 deployments/day, with 3–4 PRs in each deployment.
    - A 5–14 day experiment required 2–3 operation deployments.
    - QA and experiment operations were largely owned by engineers.

   
   
     
   
 

 

Conversations with engineers, QA, and product managers confirmed that the same workflow created different dependencies for each role.

 

The data converged on four connected system conditions.

1. Code-bound control  
   Deployment and release were treated as the same operation.
2. Engineering dependency  
   Routine experiment operations required developer intervention.
3. Unstable assignment  
   Configuration changes could alter an existing user's experience.
4. Memory-based operation  
   Monitoring progressed only when someone remembered the next step.

 The team could ship experiments, but could not reliably control, preserve, and
 monitor them across their lifecycle.
